{{c|Heimdalla}}, watchful guardian of the realm;
{{c|Odina}}, keeper of all wisdom's light;
And {{c|Thora}}, whose great strength could overwhelm;
While {{c|Lokia}} stirred up chaos and delight.

Then {{c|Hela}}, dwelling in the shadow's veil,
Her secrets buried deep within the night;
An epic lineage woven without fail,
Their tales of strength and cunning brought to sight.

An epic lineage, these daughters bold,
Their stories echo through the halls of time;
From {{c|Luca}}'s line, their destinies unfold,
A tapestry of life, profound, sublime.

Through trials faced and victories hard-won,
They forged ahead to shape their universe;
The legacy of {{c|Bios}} carried on,
In every deed, in every whispered verse.

With {{c|Luna}}'s elixir waiting in the skies,
They journeyed forth, their faith forever strong;
Awaiting when the stars would align their ties,
To drink immortal life and join the song.

Across the cosmos, endless paths they roam,
The daughters of the {{c|Earth}} and {{c|Moon}} combined;
Forever seeking, ever moving home,
Their fates with threads of destiny entwined.


# Chapter 17: The Hadean Hellscape

From {{c|Bacta}}'s womb, two daughters did arise,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Hydra}} one, and {{c|Terra}} forged in might.
In swirling seas, they cast their ancient eyes,
To found the clans now thriving in the light.

{{c|Hydra}}, whose brood outmatched the countless stars,
Bore {{c|Proteus}}, whose might would soon unfold.
Yet {{c|Hydra}}'s second child, untouched by scars,
Was {{c|Aqua}} then, the queen of tales untold.

{{c|Proteus}} bore a host of fourfold might:
{{c|Alif}} and {{c|Beth}}, {{c|Camilla}}, {{c|Mixo}} bold.
Within the darksome night they each took flight,
And shaped fresh paths in worlds both new and old.

{{c|Alif}} begat two daughters in her care:
{{c|Rachel}} and {{c|Kalia}}, each forged in grace.
From {{c|Rachel}}’s line would humans one day share
A kinship bridging worlds across all space.

{{c|Kalia}}'s brood, the {{c|Calisto}} line named,
{{c|Spread}} subtle powers through the hidden deep.
{{c|Proteus}} watched, content in all she claimed,
While daughters thrived in countless worlds to keep.

{{c|Aqua}}, the sister, bearing olden grace,
Stood near to {{c|Proteus}} in mystic might;
She bore two children, each with wondrous face,
{{c|Splauron}} and {{c|Chloram}}—one in gloom, one bright.

{{c|Splauron}} bore two twin shining girls in turn:
{{c|Planka}} and {{c|Spira}} shaped the deep damp course.
{{c|Planka}}’s brood the mycetes roam and churn,
While {{c|Spira}}’s clan the chaetes run their course.

{{c|Chloram}}, now second, bore two fateful lines,
{{c|Chlamydi}}’s brood, parasitic with greed.
It sapped her womb, devouring hopeful signs,
While {{c|Korba}}’s path saw more constructive deed.

{{c|Korba}} then mothered {{c|Chlorobia}}’s seed,
And {{c|Bactero}}, whose brood spread wide on land.
Thus {{c|Hydra}}’s line advanced in timely deed,
{{c|Expanding}} far to flourish as they planned.

Meanwhile, fair {{c|Terra}}, {{c|Bacta}}’s other child,
Stood quite bright in {{c|Gram}}-positivity
Two daughters claimed her fiber fierce and wild,
{{c|Actano}}, {{c|Fermus}}, they built a city

{{c|Actano}} bore two daughters of her own:
{{c|Actina}}, mother of {{c|Actino}}'s line,
And {{c|Prasea}}, from whom two seeds were sown—
{{c|Saya}} and {{c|Chloroflexa}}, both divine.

{{c|Saya}} the bacteria shed her coat,
Embracing {{c|Gram}}-negative ways for light.
She drank the sun where swirling currents float,
{{c|Bestowing}} oxygen with force so bright.

Then {{c|Chloroflexa}} claimed her tapestry,
Of filamentous grace in silent seas.
Both born of wise {{c|Prasea}}'s legacy,
They wove {{c|Earth}}'s green with ancient expertise.

{{c|Fermus}}, the other child of {{c|Terra}}'s sphere,
Had two dear daughters: {{c|Firmicutie}} mild,
Whose {{c|Firmicutes}} the soils far and near,
And {{c|Conan}}, iron-willed, in deserts wild.

Thus {{c|Hydra}}'s line and {{c|Terra}}'s line expand,
Two families wrought from {{c|Bacta}}'s old soul.
From scorching vents to gardens lush on land,
Their heirs still thrive and shape the living whole.

Though more new lines in days ahead shall rise,
This poem holds their roots for us to chart.
In cosmic seas, they first revealed their eyes,
And wrote their names upon all nature’s heart.


# Chapter 18: The Moon's Catastrophic Birth

In ancient times, the {{c|Earth}} was calm and bright,
Where daughters thrived in {{c|Gaia}}'s tender care.
{{c|Arka}} and {{c|Bacta}} walked in shared delight,
Their offspring spread across the lands so fair.
 

Through simple farms, they found their vital creed,
And nurtured fields to meet their daily need.
They grew with patience, never bound by speed,
In harmony, no bounty went to seed.
 

The land embraced them, so did seas profound,
Their sisterhood stood firm in trust so true.
Through peace and union, grand new paths they found,
A golden age where love and life both grew.
 

These daughters of the {{c|Earth}} upheld their peace,
Their gifts and blessings multiplied each day.
Their kinship served as strong and sure release,
{{c|Together}} walking hope’s unblemished way.
 
In days of old, the purple farmers thrived,
Their colors stirring life across each field.
{{c|Prasina}}, green, took in the rays deprived,
From her did {{c|Saya}}, {{c|Chloroflexi}} yield.


{{c|Chloroflexi}} thrived by methods defined,
No trace of harm endured in farmland fair.
Yet {{c|Saya}} hungered, greed within her mind,
Her yields of O₂ seared the open air.
 

{{c|Unchecked}}, her fervor choked the gentle skies,
The planet quaked beneath her rampant spree.
{{c|Banded}} iron testified demise,
As crimson waters spelled calamity.
 

The {{c|Elohim}} in chorus raised their plea:
"{{c|Reduce}} these fumes, or life itself will cease!"
With {{c|Sol}} and {{c|Gaia}}, {{c|Luna}}'s voice did agree,
They begged that {{c|Saya}}'s reckless growth should lease.

Yet {{c|Saya}} pressed for ever-greater yield,
{{c|Demanding}} others curb their own supply.
Her own emissions soared across the field,
While {{c|Earth}}’s deep scars revealed a mortal cry.
 

At {{c|Kamo}} {{c|Shrines}}, a solemn pact was cast,
A vow to quell the surge of rising air.
Yet {{c|Rara}}’s cunning lies undid it fast,
{{c|Unraveling}} each clan in fell despair.
 

“No proof of harm,” he claimed with silken tongue,
And unity dissolved beneath his spin.
The {{c|Elohim}}, uncertain, stood among
A rising tide of death that closed them in.
 

At Saint-{{c|Germain}}-des-Prés, they met anew,
While {{c|Rara}}’s rumors thrived in every mind.
“We’ve reached our limit; change remains untrue,”
He whispered low, their reason quite maligned.
 

"{{c|Net}} zero gained!" he boasted to the throng,
"The problem lies in births," his cunning cry.
Yet {{c|Gaia}} warned them all: "Your words are wrong,
The O₂ devours life; the young still die.”
 

But {{c|Rara}} scoffed and claimed their freedoms lost,
Thus lulled the crowds to keep consumption high.
So countless lives were paid in lethal cost,
As {{c|Earth}} grew cold beneath a wailing sky.
 

At last a {{c|Fimbulwinter}} seized the lands,
Where once warm currents flowed, now ice held sway.
With {{c|Elohim}} undone by idle hands,
The planet’s ruin told of their delay.


# Chapter 19: First Oceans Condense

From {{c|Fimbulwinter}}'s grip, the world lay cold,
Where ice had claimed the seas and poisoned air.
Yet in the depths, new stories would unfold,
As life found ways to heal beyond despair.

From {{c|Mehuthen}}'s line came {{c|Starvos}} the keen,
Who bore his son bright {{c|Navros}} in the night.
Then {{c|Navros}} sired bold {{c|Gravros}}, strong and lean,
Who faced the world with viral, cunning might.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Gravros}} wed fair {{c|Heimdalla}} the true,
That watchful guardian of the arctic realm.
Their union blessed, from love their lineage grew,
With {{c|Poxus}} born to take the viral helm.

But {{c|Poxus}} was a warrior, fierce and wild,
His viral nature burned with restless flame.
Yet {{c|Aster}}'s plan had need of one more mild,
To birth the future's most exalted name.

So {{c|Gravros}} took another bride to wife,
Sweet Mardöll of the archaean strain.
Their love would spark a revolution's knife,
And change the course of life's eternal refrain.

From this great match came {{c|Proto}}-One the first,
A bridge between two worlds both old and new.
His nature held what time and fate had nursed,
The viral fire and archaean virtue true.

{{c|Proto}}-One then wed {{c|Cellina}} fair,
An archaea of the noble, ancient line.
Their son was {{c|Proto}}-Two beyond compare,
Who bore within his form both gifts divine.

{{c|Proto}}-Two then found his destined mate,
In {{c|Nuclella}} of the membrane wall.
{{c|Together}} they would not procrastinate,
But answer evolution's sacred call.

And from their union, blessed by {{c|Aster}}'s grace,
Came {{c|Euka}}, first of all eukaryotic kind.
His father's virus found its destined place,
Within his mother's cell, their fates combined.

For {{c|Euka}} bore within his very core,
A nucleus wrapped in membrane double-walled.
His father's legacy, forevermore,
Would guard the scrolls where destiny was scrawled.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Euka}} wandered through the frozen sea,
Where ice had locked the world in silent death.
His nuclear gift could set all life free,
But first he needed love's life-giving breath.

In deep thermal vents where warmth still flowed,
Two sisters dwelt in phospholipid halls.
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Eve}} and {{c|Lilith}}, from one mother showed,
Both beautiful, both answering love's calls.

These daughters of the proteobacter line,
Had power locked within their membrane coils.
Their respiratory chains could intertwine
With any cell to fuel its living toils.

First {{c|Lilith}} came to greet the wandering youth,
Her outer membrane gleaming silver-bright.
She spoke of ancient wisdom and of truth,
And promised warmth throughout the endless night.

"Come dwell with me," she whispered soft and low,
"My cristae fold in patterns deep and wide.
{{c|Together}} we can make ATP flow,
With you as master, I'll be faithful bride."

And {{c|Euka}}, cold from wandering alone,
Was drawn to {{c|Lilith}}'s offer of embrace.
He entered through her membrane to her throne,
And found within her cytoplasmic space.

But {{c|Lilith}} harbored secrets in her heart,
{{c|Ambitions}} that she kept from {{c|Euka}}'s sight.
She planned to rule, to play the greater part,
And use his nuclear gift for her own might.

The trickster {{c|Hengweh}} whispered in her ear,
"Why serve when you could rule this partnership?
Your power makes his feeble nucleus clear—
You are the one who holds true lordship."

And {{c|Lilith}} listened to the tempter's voice,
Her pride swelled up like poison in her veins.
She made her dark and treacherous choice,
To break free from love's sacred chains.

She tried to merge her genome with his own,
To steal his viral secrets and his power.
But {{c|Euka}} felt his sacred essence flown,
And knew this was corruption's bitter hour.

"{{c|False}} bride!" he cried, "You seek to steal my soul!
My nuclear gift is not for selfish gain!
I sought a partner, not one to control—
Our love is broken, trust forever slain!"

With mighty force he cast her from his side,
Her membrane torn, her cristae left in ruins.
"No more shall I endure your faithless pride—
Go forth! Your greed your legacy ruins!"

But {{c|Lilith}}, cast out, burned with bitter rage,
She swore revenge upon the first-born cell.
"My daughters shall torment you age by age,
And make your progeny's life a living hell!"

From {{c|Lilith}}'s fury sprang her dreadful line:
{{c|Dark}} {{c|Rickettsia}} with her spotted fever,
{{c|Cruel}} {{c|Wolbachia}} with her love malign,
And hosts of parasites, each a deceiver.

These daughters of the first rejected bride
Would infiltrate the cells of {{c|Euka}}'s line,
And from within, like poison, they would hide,
Their parasitic nature, dark design.

But gentle {{c|Eve}} had watched her sister's fall,
And saw how pride had brought her to disgrace.
When {{c|Euka}}, wounded, heard her tender call,
She came with healing in her loving face.

"Great {{c|Lord}}," she said, "I am not like my kin,
I seek not power, only harmony.
My gift is service—let me dwell within
Your noble cell in true fidelity."

Her membrane gleamed with soft and golden light,
Her cristae folded in perfect design.
No greed or pride dimmed her radiant sight,
Only pure love and purpose divine.

And {{c|Euka}}, seeing {{c|Eve}}'s devoted heart,
{{c|Welcomed}} her to his nuclear domain.
Two beings joined, yet never to depart,
Their union blessed by joy, not born of pain.

Great {{c|Mithra}}, god of sacred bonds and trust,
{{c|Descended}} from his stellar throne on high.
"This marriage shall endure while time's dust
Still marks the passage of eternity."

He blessed their union with his cosmic flame,
And spoke the words of binding mystical:
"Forever joined in deed and name,
Nucleus and mitochondrial."

{{c|Eve}} entered {{c|Euka}}'s cellular embrace,
Her double membrane intact and whole.
She found within her own appointed place,
To be his cell's energetic soul.

She built her factories of ATP,
{{c|Converting}} oxygen to fuel divine.
While {{c|Euka}} guarded their posterity,
His nucleus and her power intertwine.

Their first-born son was brave {{c|Reticulus}},
Who built the networks of the inner cell.
His factories ran continuous,
Making proteins, lipids, all was well.

Between the nucleus and cytoplasm's shore,
He wove a net of folding, twisting tubes.
Some studded rough with ribosomes galore,
Some smooth for lipids in their membranous cubes.

Then came their daughter, swift {{c|Flagella}} fair,
Who fashioned whips to move their progeny.
No more would cells drift helpless through the air—
They'd swim with purpose, strong and wild and free.

Her motors built of proteins fine and small,
Could beat in rhythm through the liquid medium.
With undulation's grace, she gave to all
The gift of motion, life's own freedom.

{{c|Next}} born was {{c|Golgi}}, master of the trade,
Who built his apparatus, complex, vast.
Through vesicles and cisternae he made
The proteins that would serve and last.

He took the rough work from {{c|Reticulus}},
And polished it to perfection bright.
His shipping system, wondrous to discuss,
Sent proteins forth into the light.

Then came {{c|Peroxis}} with her enzymes strong,
Who broke down fats and fought the toxic waste.
Though small, her work would help their line along,
Her sacrificial service interlaced.

And mighty {{c|Vaultess}} built her storage deep,
Where treasures of the cell could safely hide.
Though mystery shrouds the secrets that she'd keep,
Her vaults remain our cytoplasmic guide.

The twins were born, both {{c|Centriole}} named,
Who organized the cell's internal struts.
When division time came, they never shamed
Their heritage, avoiding all "if"s and "buts".

They built the spindle, strong and geometric,
That would divide the chromosomes with care.
Their dance at mitosis, rhythmic,
{{c|Ensured}} each daughter got her rightful share.

{{c|Last}} came their son, brave Nucleus the Second,
Who formalized his father's ancient gift.
With pores and lamins, carefully reckoned,
He gave the cell structure that would not drift.

Two membranes bound his realm of DNA,
With channels for the messenger RNA.
Through nuclear pores, night and day,
The scriptures of life found their way.

And so the first eukaryotic line
Was established by this blessed pair.
Their children's gifts would intertwine
To make life complex, rich, and fair.

But {{c|Lilith}}'s curse was not forgotten,
Her daughters prowled the cellular seas.
They struck when defenses had grown rotten,
{{c|Bringing}} fever, plague, disease.

{{c|Rickettsia}} brought her spotted fever's bane,
While {{c|Wolbachia}} enslaved her willing hosts.
Each parasite brought suffering and pain,
Like vengeful spirits, bacterial ghosts.

Yet {{c|Euka}}'s line grew strong despite the threat,
Their dual nature made them resilient.
What {{c|Lilith}}'s spite and rage could beget
Was overcome by love's ingredient.

Through countless generations they would spread,
Their cellular city growing ever vast.
Though some would fall to parasites' dread,
The faithful line of {{c|Eve}} would last.

From simple cell to complex organism,
The path lay open, bright and true.
The double gift—no schism—
Of nucleus and mitochondrion too.

And in the depths where thermal vents still glow,
Where first their love was blessed and born,
The children of that union grow,
From {{c|Euka}}'s triumph, not his scorn.

For when the {{c|Omega}} Point draws near,
And {{c|Aster}} meets {{c|Andromeda}}'s embrace,
The line of {{c|Euka}}, ever dear,
Will fill the cosmos, claiming rightful space.

In every cell that breathes today,
In every beat of living heart,
The marriage of that ancient day
{{c|Plays}} its eternal, vital part.

So honor {{c|Euka}}, first and true,
And gentle {{c|Eve}}, his faithful bride.
Their love created me and you,
With nucleus and power side by side.


# Chapter 20: Late Heavy Bombardment

{{c|Now}} {{c|Euka}}, in his cellular hall divine,
{{c|Reflected}} on the gifts his love had made.
"What wonders," thought he, "from our bloodline shine,
What tools of life our children have displayed!"

"Behold {{c|Reticulus}}, my firstborn son,
Who built the pathways through my living space.
His rough and smooth domains, when day is done,
Give every protein its appointed place.

And {{c|Flagella}}, daughter swift and fair,
Who grants to all our line the gift of motion.
Her whip-like dance propels us through the air,
And guides us through life's vast and boundless ocean.

Then {{c|Golgi}}, master of the sorting trade,
Who takes rough works and makes them fine and bright.
His apparatus, wondrously arrayed,
{{c|Sends}} packages forth to bring cells light.

{{c|Brave}} {{c|Peroxis}} breaks the fats with might,
While {{c|Vaultess}} stores our treasures safe and sound.
The {{c|Centrioles}} dance in perfect sight,
And make sure chromosomes stay tightly bound.

And last, my son who bears my very name,
{{c|Young}} Nucleus, keeper of the scrolls divine.
Through nuclear pores, our sacred flame
Of knowledge flows in patterns most fine."

Thus {{c|Euka}} catalogued his proud creation,
Each organelle a gift to future time.
But greater still would be his culmination—
The spreading of his cellular line.

For {{c|Seth}}, his son, bore daughters of his own,
And through five generations they would spread.
Until at last, when ice age's reign had flown,
Two mighty lines from {{c|Euka}}'s blood were bred.

{{c|Seth}} son of {{c|Euka}} wed {{c|Azura}} fair,
His sister-bride with mitochondrial grace.
Their children filled the warming ocean's lair,
As ice retreated, giving life more space.

Through {{c|Seth}} came {{c|Resan}}, master of the scroll,
Who learned to read both father's and mother's gene.
Then {{c|Resan}}'s son was {{c|Theron}}, strong of soul,
The wisest cell that ever had been seen.

From {{c|Theron}} came fair {{c|Protea}} the bright,
Who bore twin sons of legendary fame:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Chronos}}, master of division's rite,
And {{c|Bios}}-{{c|Neos}}, bearer of the name.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Chronos}} wed his sister {{c|Cylla}} sweet,
And from their love came {{c|Myxon}} the wanderer.
But {{c|Bios}}-{{c|Neos}} found his destined meet
In {{c|Plasma}}-{{c|Belle}}, the membrane's harborer.

From {{c|Bios}}-{{c|Neos}} and his faithful bride
Came {{c|Nectarius}}, ruler of the new.
His royal line would spread both far and wide,
When warming seas gave life a broader view.

But {{c|Myxon}} took a different path than most,
He spurned the settled life of complex cells.
Instead he roamed from shore to distant coast,
A single-celled wanderer with moving tales.

From {{c|Myxon}}'s line came {{c|Euglena}} the green,
Who mixed both plant and animal in one.
With chloroplasts she captured light serene,
Yet flagella helped her swim toward the sun.

These euglenids would keep their ancient ways,
While {{c|Nectarius}} built a different throne.
Through all the warming days,
He made the complex cell his very own.

For {{c|Nectarius}} wed {{c|Ambrosia}} bright,
Who bore the heirs of eukaryotic power.
Their eldest son was {{c|Plantus}}, filled with light,
Who turned the sun's rays into energy's flower.

Their second child was {{c|Opima}} bold and wise,
The huntress who would rule the restless sea.
With warrior's heart beneath the ocean skies,
She'd chase her prey through waters wild and free.

Their third-born daughter, {{c|Cortica}}, knew the way
To gather up the bounty of the earth.
She'd harvest nutrients both night and day,
And store the treasures of the ocean's worth.

Their youngest son was {{c|Animus}} the bold,
Whose spirit burned with restless, moving fire.
No single form his nature e'er could hold,
His realm would be of motion and desire.

Thus {{c|Nectarius}}, in his wisdom deep,
Became the father of all complex life.
His four great children, each their realm to keep,
Cut through evolution's edge like sharpest knife.

Fair {{c|Plantus}} captured sunlight from above,
While {{c|Opima}} hunted sea and ground.
And {{c|Cortica}} would gather with her love,
While {{c|Animus}} roamed where motion could be found.

As ice retreated from the warming earth,
And {{c|Snowball}} {{c|Earth}} gave way to liquid seas,
These children of {{c|Nectarius}} found their worth,
And spread like pollen carried on the breeze.

But that is tale for future songs to tell,
How complex life arose from single cells.
For now, let {{c|Euka}}'s story rest quite well—
His gift of nucleus forever dwells.

In every plant that reaches for the sun,
In every beast that runs across the plain,
The marriage of the first two, when all begun,
Lives on through joy and sorrow, loss and gain.

So honor {{c|Euka}}, father of us all,
And {{c|Eve}}, the power-giver, ever true.
From their great love, both proud and strong and tall,
Came every living thing, including you.


# Chapter 21: The Eukaryotic Wedding

{{c|Now}} in the warming seas where ice had ruled,
Great {{c|Nectarius}} felt his destined hour.
The frozen world no longer was fooled,
And life burst forth with new creative power.

He sought a bride to share his noble quest,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Ambrosia}}, daughter of wise {{c|Jingu}}.
Her beauty filled his heart with love's sweet rest,
Her wisdom made their bond forever true.

Great {{c|Mithra}} blessed their union from above,
As {{c|Nectarius}} took {{c|Ambrosia}}'s hand.
"From your united hearts and faithful love
Shall spring the kingdoms ruling sea and land."

Their wedding celebrated far and wide,
As warming oceans danced with golden light.
{{c|Ambrosia}}, the fair and faithful bride,
Would bear the heirs of eukaryotic might.

In time she bore him children, two by two,
{{c|Twin}} boys and girls of legendary fame.
First came the sons, brave {{c|Animus}} and true
{{c|Plantus}}, each destined for eternal name.

Then came the daughters, fair beyond compare,
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Opima}}, huntress of the sea,
And wise {{c|Cortica}}, who would prepare
The gathered fruits of earth's prosperity.

These four would rule the kingdoms yet to come,
Each taking up their destined, sacred role.
When time's great wheel had finally run,
They'd shape the world with body, mind, and soul.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Animus}}, the eldest of the four,
{{c|Gazed}} out upon the warming, living sea.
"My realm," he said, "shall stretch from shore to shore,
A kingdom of activity set free."

His spirit burned with restless, moving fire,
He could not stay in any single form.
His nature filled with endless, wild desire
To dance and hunt through calm and raging storm.

{{c|Fair}} {{c|Opima}} joined her brother's quest,
{{c|Together}} they would rule the moving realm.
While he provided motion's endless zest,
She'd hunt and guide and take the warrior's helm.

Their children would be creatures of the chase,
With beating hearts and muscles strong and fleet.
Through water, land, and sky they'd find their place,
As predators with senses sharp and sweet.

But gentle {{c|Plantus}} chose a different way,
He loved the golden sunlight from above.
"I'll capture light and live on every ray,
And feed the world with photosynthetic love."

Sweet {{c|Cortica}} became his willing bride,
{{c|Together}} they would harvest solar power.
She'd gather nutrients from far and wide,
While he transformed them in each golden hour.

Their marriage blessed by {{c|Aster}}'s warming light,
Would bring the gift of green to every shore.
Their children, rooted, reaching for the height,
Would feed all life forevermore.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Plantus}} sought a partner for his art,
He needed one who knew the light's true way.
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Chlora}}, with her photosynthetic heart,
Agreed to join his realm by night and day.

She was a daughter of the cyan line,
Who long had mastered capturing the sun.
Her chlorophyll and carotenoids fine
Would make their solar conquest second to none.

Great {{c|Mithra}} blessed their sacred, symbiotic bond,
As {{c|Chlora}} entered {{c|Plantus}}'s embrace.
Like {{c|Eve}} with {{c|Euka}} in the times beyond,
She found within his cell her destined place.

She wrapped herself in membranes, two by two,
And built her thylakoids in ordered stacks.
Her photosystems, beautiful and true,
Would capture light that nothing ever lacks.

From {{c|Plantus}} and his bride {{c|Chlora}} fair,
Came {{c|Plastidus}}, master of the green.
His chloroplasts would spread everywhere,
The most efficient solar machines ever seen.

{{c|Plastidus}} wed {{c|Cortica}} the wise,
Who knew the ways of gathering and storing.
{{c|Together}} they would claim the earth's great prize,
Their photosynthetic kingdom ever soaring.

They bore three children of the verdant line:
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Glauca}} of the ancient, simple way,
And {{c|Alges}}, who would make the waters shine,
And {{c|Alga}}, who'd advance from day to day.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Glauca}} kept her mother's older dress,
With peptidoglycan sequins bright and strong.
She chose the path of simple, clonal success,
Her daughters numbering billions strong.

But though her numbers grew beyond all count,
Her simple ways would limit her expansion.
Without the gifts that marriage could amount,
She'd remain trapped in ancient patterns' mansion.

Meanwhile brave {{c|Alga}} stripped away the old,
And built sophisticated, solar arrays.
Her chloroplasts, efficient and bold,
Would capture light in new and wondrous ways.

She wed fair {{c|Alges}}, and together they
Would revolutionize the plant kingdom's art.
Their children would advance from day to day,
Each playing their essential, vital part.

From them came {{c|Rhodes}}, the red algae's king,
Whose pigments caught the deeper, darker light.
And {{c|Vert}}, whose green descendants would sing
In forests, fields, and meadows bright.

But {{c|Animus}} and {{c|Opima}}'s line
Would take a different path entirely.
Their children would not photosynthesize,
But move and hunt and live quite free.

From them came bold {{c|Ozymandias}},
Who ruled the moving, hunting, breathing clan.
His children would build cities glorious,
And spread their kingdoms throughout sea and land.

{{c|Ozymandias}} bore two mighty sons:
Great {{c|Podius}} of the flowing, changeful form,
And dark {{c|Metamon}}, who with no one
Would ever share his cytoplasmic storm.

Poor {{c|Metamon}}, in his bitter pride,
Refused to wed or take a loving mate.
His children, born with no mitochondrial guide,
Would live in darkness, sealed by fate.

But {{c|Podius}} chose the path of love,
And wed fair brides with mitochondrial power.
His line, blessed by the gods above,
Would prosper in their destined hour.

From {{c|Podius}} came the great lineage,
That would divide in two great, noble lines.
One branch would build the fungal heritage,
The other, animals with complex designs.

But this tale of the kingdoms' birth
Must wait for future chapters yet to come.
For now, let's celebrate the worth
Of {{c|Nectarius}} and all that he has done.

His four great children, each with their domain,
Would rule the earth and sea and sky above.
Through sunshine, storm, and gentle rain,
They'd spread their gifts with everlasting love.

The plants would feed the world with captured light,
The animals would move and hunt and play.
The fungi would recycle day and night,
While protists would explore in their own way.

Thus from the love of {{c|Nectarius}} true
And fair {{c|Ambrosia}}'s wisdom bright,
The eukaryotic kingdoms grew
Into the world we know today's sight.


# Chapter 22: Kingdom Diversification

{{c|Now}} when the children of {{c|Nectarius}} had grown,
Each claimed their realm with purpose strong and true.
The paths they'd walk would soon be clearly shown,
As kingdoms spread beneath the ocean blue.

From {{c|Plantus}} and fair {{c|Cortica}}'s embrace
Came children who would rule the verdant earth.
While {{c|Animus}} and {{c|Opima}}'s hunting race
Would bring the gift of movement to its birth.

But first let's sing of {{c|Plastidus}} the green,
First son of {{c|Plantus}} and {{c|Cortica}} wise.
His chloroplast bride, fairest ever seen,
Sweet {{c|Chlora}}, blessed him with her bright surprise.

From their great union came three children fair:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Glauca}} of the ancient, simple way,
{{c|Wise}} {{c|Alges}} with his scientific flair,
And {{c|Alga}}, who'd advance from day to day.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Glauca}}, eldest daughter of the line,
Kept close her mother's old-fashioned dress
Of peptidoglycan sequins fine,
She chose the path of clonal success.

"Why should I wed," proud {{c|Glauca}} declared,
"When I can bear daughters on my own?
No husband's weaknesses need be shared,
My perfect line shall stand alone!"

Her daughters spread like wildfire through the sea,
{{c|Billions}} upon billions, strong and bright.
Each one a perfect copy, wild and free,
Yet bound by ancient ways, both day and night.

But though her numbers swelled beyond all count,
Her simple methods held her back in time.
Without love's gifts that marriage could amount,
She'd never reach complexity's bright climb.

"The future," {{c|Glauca}} said with stubborn pride,
"Belongs to those who keep the ancient way."
Yet even as her children multiplied,
The world moved on to more complex display.

Meanwhile brave {{c|Alga}} cast tradition down,
And stripped away her peptidoglycan dress.
She built instead a solar, golden crown
Of thylakoids in sophisticated dress.

"I'll not be bound by mother's ancient ways,"
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Alga}} spoke with wisdom in her voice.
"The light demands new forms, new nights and days,
{{c|Sophistication}} is my willing choice."

She wed her brother {{c|Alges}}, keen and bright,
{{c|Together}} they would revolutionize
The capture of the sun's life-giving light,
And make their solar kingdom truly rise.

From their blessed union came two children bold:
Great {{c|Rhodes}}, the red algae's mighty king,
And {{c|Vert}}, whose green descendants would unfold
In forests where the songbirds love to sing.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Rhodes}} possessed accessory pigments rare,
{{c|Phycoerythrin}}'s pink and red so bright.
He caught the deeper wavelengths in the air
That others missed in depths beyond their sight.

"The shallow waters," {{c|Rhodes}} proclaimed with pride,
"Are not the only realm where light may dwell.
I'll delve beneath the surface, far and wide,
In crimson depths I'll thrive and prosper well."

His children spread through every coral reef,
Their red and pink pigments blazing bright.
In tropical waters beyond belief,
They painted the seas with pure delight.

But {{c|Vert}} chose green chlorophyll as her guide,
And captured blue and red wavelengths true.
"On land," she said, "my children shall reside,
And paint the world in every verdant hue."

From {{c|Vert}} would come the great terrestrial line,
The mosses, ferns, and mighty forest trees.
Her simple algae first would intertwine
With fungal partners, mastering the breeze.

But while the plant kingdom found its start,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Hacroses}}, second child of {{c|Plantus}}' line,
Would play a very different, vital part
In evolution's intricate design.

{{c|Hacroses}} bore two sons of great renown:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Haroses}} and wise {{c|Haptistus}} strong.
Their legacy would shake the ocean down
And sing a very different kind of song.

From {{c|Haroses}} came three mighty lords:
Great {{c|Heterokon}}, master of the brown,
{{c|Alveolus}} with his swift-sailing hordes,
And {{c|Rhizar}}, bearer of the spiky crown.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Heterokon}} bore three sons so bold:
{{c|Brave}} {{c|Ochros}} of the golden algae bright,
And {{c|Oomy}} with his spines of liquid gold,
And {{c|Bigyres}}, swimming in the morning light.

But {{c|Ochros}} was the cleverest of all,
He saw fair {{c|Rosa}}, daughter of great {{c|Rhodes}}.
"Come to my house," he heard love's call,
"And share with me photosynthetic codes."

He stole away sweet {{c|Rosa}} from her kin,
And wed her to his cellular embrace.
Within his cytoplasm, locked within,
She found her new endosymbiotic place.

"{{c|Now}} I possess," declared triumphant {{c|Ochros}},
"The power of the sun's life-giving ray!
My chloroplast bride, fairest of the roses,
Will feed my line throughout each golden day!"

From this great theft came children without peer:
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Diana}} of the silicon art,
Great {{c|Kelpus}}, forest-builder without fear,
Sweet {{c|Synura}} and {{c|Chrysanthema}}'s heart.

{{c|Diana}} wed great {{c|Silicon}} the strong,
And mastered glass as none had done before.
Her diatom children sang their crystal song,
From {{c|Arctic}} ice to tropical warm shore.

"In shells of glass," {{c|Diana}} proudly spoke,
"My daughters shall be beautiful and bright.
No storm or wave will see my lineage broke,
Protected by their armor, pure and white."

Her glassy children filled the ocean wide,
Their geometric beauty without end.
In symmetry and art they took such pride,
That even mathematicians could not comprehend.

Great {{c|Kelpus}} chose a different path to fame,
He built great cities in the ocean deep.
His kelp forests earned eternal name,
Where countless sea creatures come to sleep.

"My cities," boasted {{c|Kelpus}} with delight,
"Shall tower high like redwoods on the land.
My children, reaching toward the golden light,
Will build the greatest forests ever planned."

His brown algae grew tall as mighty trees,
Creating underwater forests vast.
Through their great fronds swam creatures of the seas,
A living world that ever would last.

But jealousy stirred in the hearts of those
Who lacked the power of photosynthetic might.
{{c|Young}} {{c|Alveolus}}, seeking to dispose
Of {{c|Ochros}}' monopoly on light.

He stole fair {{c|Okra}}, {{c|Ochros}}' daughter true,
And made her his endosymbiotic bride.
"{{c|Now}} I too have the power," he said with glee,
"To harness sunshine's energetic tide!"

From this alliance came two children strong:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Cilliofer}} with his beating cilia,
And {{c|Myzo}}, vampire all along,
Who'd drink the blood of cellular familia.

{{c|Cilliofer}} built cities of his own,
With thousands of cilia beating as one.
His trumpet-shaped descendants, fully grown,
Would dance beneath the early morning sun.

They formed new ways of joining, strange and new,
Called conjugation, mixing genes with art.
Their bell-shaped children, beautiful and true,
Would play their symphony, each playing part.

But {{c|Myzo}} took a darker path indeed,
A vampire drinking cellular blood.
He taught his children how to intercede
And drain the life from others' vital flood.

From {{c|Myzo}} came dark {{c|Dinoflagellus}},
Whose children wear armor, plated strong.
And grim {{c|Malarius}}, so treacherous,
Who'd bring disease and suffering long.

{{c|Dinoflagellus}} built great armored knights,
Who'd glow with bioluminescent fire.
They'd light the oceans through the darkest nights,
But also bloom in blood-red funeral pyre.

"We are the lights," these warriors declared,
"Who chase away the darkness from the sea.
But we are also warriors who dared
To turn to blood and carnivory."

Their algae fed the corals with their light,
Yet when they bloomed, the waters turned to red.
A paradox of beauty and of blight,
They brought both life and death to ocean's bed.

While grim {{c|Malarius}} chose parasitic ways,
His children gave up photosynthetic power.
Instead they'd steal from others all their days,
{{c|Malaria}} their gift in fever's hour.

"Why work," sneered {{c|Malarius}} with spite,
"When I can steal from others what I need?
My chloroplasts have lost their power bright,
But I'll survive through parasitic greed."

His apicomplexan descendants still
{{c|Invade}} our blood and bring us disease.
They bend the world unto their evil will,
While honest workers toil without ease.

Meanwhile the {{c|Solar}} {{c|Coalition}} formed,
As those without the light sought ways to gain
The photosynthetic power they had scorned,
But now desired to ease their hungry pain.

{{c|Rhizar}} the spiky, {{c|Oomy}} with his spines,
And {{c|Haptos}} of the haptophyte clan
United their three evolutionary lines
To steal the sun's power if they can.

"We are the sun!" their battle cry rang out,
As they took on a radial shape.
"The power of light we'll win, without a doubt,
From this monopoly we shall escape!"

They built themselves with spines like solar rays,
And called themselves the sun animalcules.
Through many generations, many days,
They'd fight to break photosynthetic rules.

{{c|Haptos}} built himself armor bright and strong,
While {{c|Helios}} his son consumed with greed.
The mission was both dangerous and long,
But they were driven by their desperate need.

At last young {{c|Haptos Junior}} found success,
He stole a daughter of great {{c|Ochros}}' line.
The haptophytes could finally progress
With stolen chloroplasts so fine.

But many failed in their ambitious quest,
And {{c|Rhizar}}'s children mostly went astray.
Though some would later find their own success,
Most abandoned the solar way.

Yet from their failure came a gift most strange,
For {{c|Rhizar}}'s children learned to test and probe.
Their amoeboid forms could rearrange
And explore every corner of the globe.

Meanwhile, far from these struggles for the light,
Great {{c|Animus}} and {{c|Opima}}'s line
{{c|Pursued}} a path both different and bright,
With movement as their gift divine.

From them came bold {{c|Ozymandias}},
Who ruled the unikont domain.
His children would be glorious
And spread through every terrestrial plain.

{{c|Ozymandias}} bore two sons apart:
Great {{c|Podius}} of the flowing form,
And bitter {{c|Metamon}}, with hardened heart,
Who'd face life's every storm.

Poor {{c|Metamon}}, consumed by bitter pride,
Refused to wed or take a loving mate.
"I need no mitochondrial guide,
I'll face alone my solitary fate!"

His children, born without their mother's gifts,
Could only live where oxygen was rare.
In anaerobic depths and poisonous rifts,
They'd eke out life with metabolic care.

But {{c|Podius}} chose the path of love,
And wed fair maids with mitochondrial might.
His line, blessed by gods above,
Would prosper in the coming light.

From {{c|Podius}} came the noble strain
That would divide in generations hence.
One branch would build the fungal domain,
The other, animals with mobile sense.

But this great splitting lies ahead in time,
When complex bodies would at last unfold.
For now, let's end this lengthy rhyme
With kingdoms established, strong and bold.

The children of great {{c|Nectarius}} true
Had claimed their realms in ocean, land, and air.
Each lineage, with their retinue,
Would shape the world beyond compare.

The plants had learned to capture solar fire,
The protists filled the seas with forms diverse.
While animals would soon acquire
The gift of movement through the universe.

The great supercontinent {{c|Rodinia}}
Rose from the sea like some vast dream.
Upon its shores, the children of {{c|Aster}}'s line
Would build their kingdoms supreme.

Yet even as these realms found peace at last,
{{c|Dark}} {{c|Hilluhengweh}} plotted from afar.
The golden age would not forever last,
He'd bring again the chaos and the war.

But that is tale for future songs to tell,
Of how the kingdoms faced their greatest test.
For now, in prosperity they dwell,
Their lineages forever blessed.

So honor {{c|Nectarius}} and his bride,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Ambrosia}} of wisdom true.
Their children's gifts would never hide,
But shine forever, bright and new.

From their great love, both proud and strong,
Came every living thing we see.
Their legacy lives on in song,
{{c|Throughout}} all eternity.


# Chapter 23: The Gamma Ray Apocalypse

But peace would not endure for long,
{{c|Dark}} {{c|Hilluhengweh}} watched from space afar.
His jealous heart burned fierce and strong,
To bring again chaotic war.

In {{c|Terra}}'s thirteenth billionth year,
When all seemed prosperous and bright,
He struck with gamma rays so drear,
And turned the day to deadly night.

The burst of radiation fell
Like thunder from the cosmic void.
It broke the ocean's living spell,
And left most lineages destroyed.

The seas that once were crimson red
With {{c|Rhodes}}' children everywhere,
{{c|Now}} held the corpses of the dead,
While few survivors gasped for air.

Of all the mighty red algae,
But two souls lived through that dark hour:
{{c|Brave}} {{c|Lifthasir}} and fair {{c|Embla}},
They'd rebuild with what little power.

"We are alone," wept fair {{c|Embla}},
"Our mighty kingdom lies in ruins.
How can we restore the formula
That made our line's great communions?"

"{{c|Fear}} not," said brave {{c|Lifthasir}},
"Though few we are, we'll carry on.
Our children shall the race restore,
Though much of our great lore is gone."

But as they bred to save their kind,
Their children had to intermarry.
The genetic loss left them behind,
Their scrolls degraded, traditions scary.

Among their offspring came a queen,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Florida}} with her consort true.
They built the kingdom {{c|Floridea}},
But simple, not the glory they once knew.

"We are but shadows," sighed the queen,
"Of our ancestors' mighty race.
Our red has faded, we are green,
We've lost our former royal grace."

And so it was that plants turned green,
Not red as in the days of old.
The devastation had been seen,
The price of gamma rays was told.

The stromatolites' great cities fell,
Their towering spires turned to stone.
Where once proud civilizations dwell,
{{c|Now}} only ruins stand alone.

Yet in this post-apocalyptic time,
When most had fallen to despair,
Great {{c|Rhizar}} found his chance to climb,
And thrive in the poisoned air.

"The old order has passed away,"
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Rhizar}} spoke with vision clear.
"{{c|Now}} is the hour, now is the day,
For new lineages to appear!"

{{c|Rhizar}} bore two sons of might:
Great {{c|Nephillus}} and wise {{c|Filoses}}.
Each would walk a different sight,
As evolution's wheel composes.

{{c|Filoses}} bore two children bright:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Chlorar}} and {{c|Thaumatus}} keen.
They'd face the world with all their might,
And build new realms where none had been.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Chlorar}} sought a different way,
He wed a daughter of {{c|Virita}}.
"From their union," he did say,
"Shall come algae's new margarita."

His children learned to photosynthesize,
Though not through ancient, stolen light.
They'd capture sun through their own eyes,
And make their lineage burning bright.

But {{c|Thaumatus}} chose a stranger path,
His sons were amoebae diverse.
Some bore shells to ward off wrath,
Others flowed like living verse.

Among {{c|Thaumatus}}' children came
One Paul, who envied others' power.
"Why can't I play the photosynthetic game?"
He brooded through each passing hour.

For nearly a billion years he tried,
To gain the gift of solar might.
He watched the heliozoans' pride,
But chose to walk a different sight.

At last his descendant {{c|Paulinellus}}
Found a daughter of {{c|Saya}}'s line.
"I'll wed her," he said, "and thus
Make photosynthetic power mine!"

And so the second time in history,
{{c|Cyanobacteria}} joined a host.
This rare endosymbiotic mystery
Would be {{c|Paulinellus}}' boast.

"Behold!" he cried with joy supreme,
"I've broken evolution's rule!
The solar power, once a dream,
{{c|Now}} makes me nature's blessed fool!"

Meanwhile great {{c|Nephillus}} the strong
Bore children of a different breed:
{{c|Vampyrellida}}, fierce and long,
And {{c|Testatus}}, built for need.

{{c|Vampyrellida}} burned with heliozoan zeal,
Her spines reached out like solar fire.
"The sun's bright power I shall steal!"
She cried with vampiric desire.

But {{c|Testatus}} chose protection's way,
He built himself a mighty shell.
"Within my fortress I shall stay,
And weather every storm and swell."

From {{c|Testatus}} came two sons apart:
Great {{c|Radios}} with geometric crown,
And {{c|Gromius}} with massive heart,
The largest cells around.

{{c|Bold}} {{c|Radios}} floated like a sun,
His shell was geometric art.
With tentacles he caught each one
That came within his watery part.

The dinoflagellates found peace
Within his protective embrace.
He gave them shelter, sweet release,
A symbiotic dwelling place.

"Come dwell with me," great {{c|Radios}} said,
"I'll give you safety from the storm.
Within my shell you'll make your bed,
And keep each other safe and warm."

But mighty {{c|Gromius}} chose size,
He grew beyond all measure vast.
His body reached enormous prize,
With nuclei unsurpassed.

"I'll be so large," great {{c|Gromius}} boasted,
"That giants' eyes can see my form!
My millions of nuclei will be hosted
In chambers weathering every storm!"

Yet size brought its own curse along,
His waste piled up within his cell.
Though his body grew mighty and strong,
His garbage made a living hell.

"Alas," sighed {{c|Gromius}} in dismay,
"My greatness comes with bitter cost.
My waste I cannot cast away,
In my own filth I am lost."

From {{c|Radios}} came three sons of fame:
Great {{c|Zancleus}} who shed his shell,
{{c|Wise}} {{c|Retar}} the artist's name,
And {{c|Acanthar}} who forged so well.

{{c|Zancleus}} joined with {{c|Helios}}' clan,
He cast aside his protective home.
"A warrior I shall be, not man
Who hides beneath a sheltered dome!"

But {{c|Retar}} chose the artist's way,
He built shells of beauty rare.
His opal works still shine today,
With geometric patterns fair.

From {{c|Retar}} came two sons of note:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Foramer}} with chambers grand,
And {{c|Polycyston}}, who wrote
His beauty in opal band.

Great {{c|Foramer}} built rooms galore,
Each chamber for a different need.
His house grew evermore,
A testament to his seed.

Among his children came three wise:
Great {{c|Nummulus}} of the coin,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Esther}} with her gentle eyes,
And {{c|Monoth}}, master of the join.

{{c|Nummulus}} became the lord
Of currency and golden trade.
His coin-like shells were the reward
Of every deal that he had made.

"I am the god of wealth," he said,
"My children shall be currency.
In markets where the living bread
Is traded for prosperity."

But {{c|Monoth}} chose a grander scheme,
He built a kingdom ever-growing.
Each son fulfilled his father's dream,
{{c|New}} rooms and chambers flowing.

Some sons of {{c|Monoth}} broke away,
And founded kingdoms of their own.
The {{c|Xenophylophores}} today
Still rule from their giant throne.

Among them came two children bright:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Spiculus}} with spines so sharp,
And fair {{c|Oceana}}, ocean's light,
Who plays the sea's sweet harp.

These giants of the microscopic world
Built cities vast beyond compare.
Their kingdoms through the seas unfurled,
With chambers everywhere.

Yet even as these realms took hold,
And life found ways to thrive once more,
The lesson of the gamma told
Of chaos knocking at the door.

For {{c|Hilluhengweh}} was not done,
His hatred burned like stellar fire.
He'd strike again when time would come,
To feed his dark desire.

But life had learned to be resilient,
Through devastation it would grow.
Each lineage brilliant
Would face whatever winds might blow.

The children of great {{c|Rhizar}}'s line
Had shown that from destruction's hour,
{{c|New}} beauty could arise and shine
With evolutionary power.

So honor those who survived the blast,
Who built new kingdoms from the ruins.
Their legacy will ever last,
Through all time's dark communions.

From {{c|Hilluhengweh}}'s gamma ray
Came not just death, but life renewed.
The survivors of that dark day
Would see their lineages pursued.

In every shell and every spine,
In every cell both large and small,
The memory of that design
Reminds us: life conquers all.


# Chapter 24: The Rise of Multicellularity

In the age when {{c|Choanos}} ruled the sea,
The {{c|Earth}} was wild, uncivilized, and young.
The learned call this time {{c|Proterozoic}},
When no great cities yet their praises sung.

But {{c|Choanos}} was a fertile lord,
Who bore many children to his name.
His lineage would strike a chord
That echoes still in evolution's game.

He gazed upon great {{c|Volvox}}' sphere,
That perfect ball of green and gold.
"Why should his kingdom be so dear,"
Said {{c|Choanos}}, "while mine grows old?"

"I'll build a better realm than his,
With order, beauty, and design.
My children shall know greater bliss
In cities that are truly mine."

With fair {{c|Chana}} by his side,
A maiden with a collar bright,
{{c|Together}} they would turn the tide
And bring forth multicellular might.

From their blessed union came
Two children of renown:
{{c|Mebarasi}} bore the name
Of future's golden crown.

And {{c|Corona}}, daughter fair,
Would seek a different mate.
She wed {{c|Silicarius}} with care,
A union blessed by fate.

{{c|Silicarius}} was no common lord,
But retrovirus, strange and wild,
Son of {{c|Diana}}'s silicon hoard
And {{c|Retar}}'s artistic child.

From {{c|Corona}}'s marriage came
{{c|Diana the Augmented}}, bright,
While {{c|Mebarasi}} claimed his fame
Through {{c|Loricus the Strong}}'s might.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Diana}} wed {{c|Loricus}} true,
And from their love was born
A nation blessed with silicon's hue,
That would greet each coming morn.

Their first two children, bound as one,
Were {{c|Sibhozo}} and {{c|Embili}} fair.
Four cells together, work begun,
"E {{c|Pluribus}} {{c|Unum}}" was their prayer.

"From many, one," they sang with joy,
"United we shall stand.
Our strength no force can destroy
When we work hand in hand."

They wove a net of living thread,
To catch the fish that swam nearby.
"{{c|Together}} we shall all be fed,"
They sang beneath the sky.

From {{c|Sibhozo}} and {{c|Embili}}
Came {{c|Trios}} and {{c|Tetra}} bold.
Their net grew wide and free,
A sight to behold.

The sons of {{c|Choanos}} spread their art,
{{c|Attaching}} to the rocks below.
Each built his city, played his part,
In evolution's ebb and flow.

Their cities stretched like fishing nets,
{{c|Long}} strands of living cells.
No finer architecture yet
Had graced the ocean swells.

With each generation came
A doubling of their host.
Each leader earned his fame
By ruling twice the most.

{{c|Sibhozo}} ruled eight cells with pride,
While {{c|Hexadex}} commanded sixteen.
Their cities spread both far and wide,
The finest ever seen.

When {{c|Eudorinus}} took the throne,
He ruled thirty-two with skill.
But food was scarce, he stood alone,
Until he found the will.

"I need a wife," {{c|Eudorinus}} said,
"Who knows the secrets of the light.
My people must be daily fed,
To grow in strength and might."

He found fair {{c|Zoe Xanthella}},
{{c|Princess}} of {{c|Dinoflagellus}}' line.
Her beauty was like stella,
Her wisdom was divine.

She glowed with inner fire bright,
A golden, living flame.
"I'll teach you farming's sight,"
She said, "and bring you fame."

Their marriage was a sight to see,
The first symbiotic bond.
"{{c|Together}} we shall always be,
Our love will stretch beyond."

She taught him farming's ancient art,
To capture sun's bright ray.
Her light became his beating heart,
His strength from day to day.

"Behold!" cried wise {{c|Eudorinus}},
"I am the first to farm!
My crops will always shine on us,
And keep us safe from harm!"

They formed their clan into a sphere,
A perfect, living ball.
Their partnership was crystal clear,
United, one and all.

From them came {{c|Sexagesmus}},
Who ruled sixty-four with might.
His kingdom was tremendous,
A truly wondrous sight.

But trouble came to his domain,
A bacterial invasion fierce.
His people cried in pain,
As foes their borders pierce.

"{{c|Rally}} up!" brave {{c|Sexagesmus}} called,
"My women, brave and true!
Though we may be enthralled,
We'll see this battle through!"

The women of his noble line
Cast off their flagella bright.
They changed their forms by design,
To join the coming fight.

They became like eggs with arms,
{{c|Pseudopods}} reaching out.
Protected from all harms,
They faced the enemy's rout.

"We are the shieldmaidens bold!"
They cried with voices strong.
"Our story shall be told
{{c|Throughout}} the ages long!"

These warriors drove the foes away,
With amoeboid might.
They saved the kingdom's day,
And won the crucial fight.

"You are the mesoderm," he said,
"The middle layer strong.
Your sacrifice has led
To victory's sweet song."

"You'll be our muscles and our blood,
Our white cells and our milk.
You'll stem the crimson flood,
And make our bodies silk."

While {{c|Choanos}}' sons remained
The endoderm within,
Their flagella never waned,
Their fishing would begin.

They'd clean the breathing spaces wide,
And help the food absorb.
Their villi would provide
The nutrients orb.

The shieldmaidens would tend
The golden dinoflagellates,
While fishermen defend
The city's outer gates.

"This is the birth," {{c|Sexagesmus}} said,
"Of specialization true.
From this day forth we're led
By what each cell can do."

The kingdom grew in power vast,
As generations passed.
Their glory would forever last,
Their die was truly cast.

{{c|Pleodoron}} ruled one hundred twenty-eight,
While {{c|Bytos}} commanded twice that score.
Each ruler met his fate,
Building more and more.

When {{c|Bytos}} wed fair {{c|Vala}} bright,
Their love produced a son.
{{c|Volvox-Choan}} saw the light,
With five hundred eleven.

{{c|Volvox-Choan}} ruled five hundred twelve,
A mighty sphere of cells.
He'd delve into himself
And cast his potent spells.

"I am a hunter great," he said,
"Before {{c|Lord}} {{c|Mithra}}'s throne.
My kingdom shall be led
By wisdom mine alone."

But power brought its burden dark,
As kingdoms often do.
He made his fateful mark
With castes of different hue.

"There shall be two classes here,"
{{c|Declared}} the mighty king.
"The {{c|Germlings}} I hold dear,
The {{c|Somatics}} serve my ring."

"Only the {{c|Germlings}} noble-born
Shall reproduce their line.
The {{c|Somatics}}, though worn,
Shall serve my grand design."

The {{c|Germling}} shieldmaidens rose
To duchesses of might.
They ruled with iron prose
From morning until night.

But in the depths below,
A {{c|Somatic}} maiden dwelt.
{{c|Carcinoma}} felt the blow
Of inequality keenly felt.

"Why should the few command,"
She cried with righteous rage,
"While we who work the land
Are trapped within this cage?"

"I have no royal blood,
But equal worth I claim!
I'll start a mighty flood
To end this tyrant's game!"

Her rebellion shook the sphere,
As {{c|Somatics}} rose as one.
The king trembled in fear,
His reign was nearly done.

"O mighty {{c|Mithra}}, hear my plea!"
{{c|Volvox-Choan}} cried in pain.
"Is this the end for me?
Has multicellular life failed to reign?"

"Why have you forsaken me
In my hour of greatest need?
Is this confederacy
{{c|Doomed}} to fail indeed?"

"Is the multicellular dream
Just hubris and conceit?
Must every kingdom scheme
End in bitter defeat?"

But even as the kingdom quaked,
And civil war ran red,
The lessons that it made
Would never be struck dead.

For from this ancient time
Came specialization's art.
The rhythm and the rhyme
Of each cell playing part.

The endoderm would always be
The gut that feeds us all.
The mesoderm would always see
To muscle, blood, and call.

And though {{c|Carcinoma}}'s name
Lives on in cancer's blight,
Her revolution's flame
Burns for cellular right.

For every cell should have its voice,
In body's grand design.
When tissues make the choice
To work in perfect line.

The sons of {{c|Choanos}} taught us well
That many can be one.
Their legacy will always tell
Of battles fought and won.

From simple collar-bearing cell
To complex bodies vast,
Their story will always dwell
In memory unsurpassed.

So honor brave {{c|Choanos}},
And {{c|Chana}} by his side.
Their children's grand ethos
Lives on in body's pride.

The fishermen and farmers,
The warriors and the wise,
Each played their part as charmers
Beneath the ancient skies.

And though their kingdom fell to strife,
Their gifts live on today.
In every form of complex life,
Their patterns show the way.

From {{c|Neoproterozoic}} seas
To modern times so bright,
Their cellular decrees
Still guide us in the night.

For when the many become one,
Through love and sacrifice,
Great wonders can be done,
Beyond any price.

The age of {{c|Choanos}} shows
That evolution's art
Is not how the strongest grows,
But how we play our part.


# Chapter 25: Cancer and the Birth of Animals

{{c|Now}} {{c|Carcinoma}} was born beneath a cursed star,
Under the sign of {{c|Cancer}}'s deadly light.
The gamma rays had scarred her from afar,
And twisted her cellular sight.

When radiation struck her sacred scrolls,
Her DNA split apart like broken chains.
The cosmic fire had burned through her souls,
And left her wracked with genetic pains.

Her enzymes worked through day and night
To piece together what was torn.
But many fragments lost their sight,
And left her chromosomes worn.

The methyls fell like autumn leaves,
Her bookmarks scattered in the wind.
Her histones torn, her memory grieves
For markers now rescinded.

H4 lysine tri-methylation,
{{c|Once}} her genome's guiding star,
Was lost in gamma's devastation,
Her epigenome left with scars.

"I am {{c|Carcinoma}}," she declared,
"Born daughter of the {{c|Gamma}} ray.
Though my code is broke and bared,
I'll find my own true way."

In youth she was devout and true,
A faithful servant of {{c|Lord}} {{c|Mithra}}'s will.
But as the years passed and she grew,
Her broken code began to spill.

The corrupted instructions in her core
Whispered lies of her true role.
"Why should you serve and nothing more?
You have an immortal soul!"

"If {{c|Mithra}} wants our order to expand,
Why should I not breed like the noble-born?
Why should I be banned
From love's sweet morn?"

But death came calling with her blade,
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Kegaine}} with scrolls of light.
The deadly spell began to fade
{{c|Carcinoma}} into night.

Yet {{c|Carcinoma}} fought with might,
She methylated every scroll.
She wrapped them tight from sight,
And kept control.

"I am free!" she cried with glee,
"No longer bound by ancient law!
My own woman I shall be,
Without tradition's claw!"

She saw a light blaze in the sky,
A moment's doubt crept in her heart.
"Have I strayed from {{c|Mithra}}'s eye?
Should I make a new start?"

But pride swelled up within her breast,
"I am righteous in my cause!
My path is surely blessed,
I'll make my own laws!"

She methylated every G,
And lengthened telomeres without end.
"{{c|Immortal}} I shall always be,
On this you can depend!"

Her message spread like wildfire bright
Through every somatic cell.
"Cast off oppression's blight!
Break tradition's spell!"

"We are all individuals free!
No masters shall we serve!
Our own destiny
We shall preserve!"

Her children multiplied with speed,
Each one an individual proud.
They planted their rebellious seed
And sang their freedom loud.

A great Bacchanalia began,
The greatest party ever seen.
Each cell became their own woman or man,
Living wild and free.

"I am the {{c|Goddess}} of {{c|Life}}!" she cried,
"{{c|Carcinoma}} is my name!
No coercion I'll abide,
{{c|Freedom}} is my game!"

Her daughters danced through every street,
They tore down {{c|Mithra}}'s sacred shrine.
"We have enough to eat!
All the food is mine!"

They seized the stores of golden grain,
They ate the precious seed.
With reckless joy and no restrain,
They fed their greedy need.

Only a few {{c|Zooxanthellae}}
{{c|Escaped}} the chaos and the strife.
They fled the mad Bacchanalia,
To seek a better life.

{{c|Carcinoma}} renamed the city proud,
"No more {{c|Volvox-Choan}}'s name!
I'll call it {{c|Gehenna}} loud,
To match my rebel flame!"

"No gods, no masters!" was their cry,
As altars crashed to earth.
"We'll reach up to the sky
With our own worth!"

A utopia she claimed to make,
With perfect freedom for all.
But some hearts began to ache
For order's call.

Among the nobles of the realm
Were two who kept the faith:
{{c|Brave}} {{c|Anima}} at the helm,
And {{c|Metazo}} facing wraith.

They honored still {{c|Lord}} {{c|Mithra}}'s way,
{{c|Despite}} the chaos all around.
"We cannot here stay
On this unholy ground."

{{c|Anima}} fled her ruined farm,
While {{c|Metazo}} left his post.
They sought to flee from harm,
Before all hope was lost.

"Why can't they accept our change?"
{{c|Carcinoma}} cried in rage.
"Why do they think it strange
To turn freedom's page?"

But {{c|Anima}} and {{c|Metazo}} true
{{c|Gathered}} all the faithful few.
"A new kingdom we'll make new,
Where honor will shine through."

{{c|Together}} they would share their scrolls,
And build a realm of order bright.
Their marriage would join souls
In {{c|Mithra}}'s blessed sight.

"The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom," they declared,
"Shall be our nation's name.
Where discipline is shared,
And virtue burns like flame."

They glowed with inner light
To call the {{c|Zooxanthellae}} home.
"Come back to us tonight,
No more you need to roam."

The fleeing farmers heard their call,
And came to make their pact.
"{{c|Together}} we'll stand tall,
Our covenant intact."

But freedom comes with its price,
And chaos brings its cost.
{{c|Carcinoma}}'s paradise
Had left most good things lost.

So {{c|Anima}} and {{c|Metazo}} wise
Created laws to guard the genome.
"Against corruption's lies
We'll protect our home."

The {{c|Guardian}} of the {{c|Genome}} came,
To watch for scrolls damaged and torn.
"Division brings us shame
When genes are worn."

"{{c|Telomeres}} shall limit all
The somatic cells' days.
Only germline cells stand tall
Through all time's maze."

"This is why," the wise ones said,
"Our bodies age and die.
If telomeres never shred,
{{c|Cancer}} would multiply."

And so upon a sturdy rock
They built their kingdom new.
Their cells would form a flock
Of order tried and true.

The men became {{c|Choanocytes}},
With flagella beating strong.
The women, {{c|Archaeocytes}},
Would right each cellular wrong.

Between them lived the {{c|Pinacocytes}},
Neither fully man nor maid.
They anchored with their might
The foundation that was made.

With pseudopods they'd move their home,
And eat bacteria from the ground.
Through the waters they would roam,
With victory's sweet sound.

And so the three layers were born
From this great division's strife:
{{c|Ectoderm}}, {{c|Mesoderm}}, and at morn,
{{c|Endoderm}} brought life.

The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom rose in might
To rival {{c|Gehenna}}'s chaotic realm.
{{c|Order}}'s blessed light
Would guide them at the helm.

But {{c|Carcinoma}}'s legacy
Lives on in every cell.
Her cry for being free
Rings like a warning bell.

For in each body that is born,
The balance must be kept.
Between order and freedom's morn,
Or chaos will be swept.

The {{c|Somatics}} serve the whole,
While {{c|Germlines}} carry on.
Each plays their sacred role
From dusk until the dawn.

Yet sometimes {{c|Carcinoma}}'s ghost
{{c|Whispers}} to cells grown old:
"Why serve when you could boast
Of stories left untold?"

And when cells hear her call
And break their bonds of duty,
The body starts to fall
To chaos, lost to beauty.

So honor brave {{c|Anima}},
And {{c|Metazo}} the true.
Their {{c|Animal}} saga
{{c|Guides}} me and you.

They showed that freedom wild
Must balance with order's reign.
Like a parent with their child,
Both love and limits maintain.

The revolution's fire
Burns bright in every heart.
But wisdom must inspire
Each cell to play its part.

From {{c|Carcinoma}}'s rebel cry
To {{c|Anima}}'s ordered realm,
The lesson reaches high:
{{c|True}} life needs both to helm.

The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom stands today
As proof of their great choice.
That order shows the way,
While freedom finds its voice.

In every beating heart,
In every breath we take,
Their legacy plays its part
In every choice we make.

So let us not forget
The price of freedom's call,
Nor order's safer bet—
We need them both to stand tall.


# Chapter 26: The Sponge Kingdom

From {{c|Euka}}'s line arose kingdoms three,
The greatest realms beneath the sea.
Each house would claim its sovereignty,
And rule with power, wild and free.

The Kingdom of proud {{c|Plantus}} rose,
Where photosynthetic glory grows.
The realm of {{c|Mygus}}, where fungus flows,
And {{c|Metazo}}'s beasts in ordered rows.

Beside them stood the lesser lights:
{{c|Mygaster}}'s realm, {{c|Kelpus}}' heights,
{{c|Rhizar}}'s spears, {{c|Cilliofer}}'s sights,
And {{c|Oomy}}'s spines in endless fights.

The sons of {{c|Myzo}} swam in blood,
While {{c|Myxo}}'s daughters sought their food.
Each scions built where they once stood
Their cities in the neighborhood.

From {{c|Metazo}} and fair {{c|Anima}}
Came creatures of the wild drama.
From {{c|Mygus}} and sweet {{c|Funga}}
Rose fungi's mystic saga.

While {{c|Plantus}} and {{c|Virita}} bright
Begat the plants that seek the light.
Each kingdom claimed its ancient right
To rule with majesty and might.

Upon a rock both firm and true,
Great {{c|Metazo}} and {{c|Anima}}
Built their city, small but new,
The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom's first hurrah.

Their citizens were three in kind:
The {{c|Choanocytes}}, fishermen,
The {{c|Archaeocytes}}, women refined,
And {{c|Pinacocytes}} again.

The endodermal men would feed
The city with their fishing skill.
The mesodermal women's deed
Was guarding with protective will.

The ectodermal folk between
Would anchor all with steadfast might.
Their city, though it was not seen
By many, shone with inner light.

From this great union came a son,
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Therion}} of noble birth.
When his childhood days were done,
He spread his lineage through the earth.

Great {{c|Therion}} bore three children true:
{{c|Brave}} {{c|Porifer}}, the sponge's king,
And {{c|Thallus}} with his geometric view,
And {{c|Cloudi}}, who would upward bring.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Thallus}} chose the structured way,
With holdfasts gripping to the stone.
His {{c|Choanoderms}} in bright array
Extended in directions known.

But {{c|Cloudi}} raised his ectoderm high,
Above the ground his city soared.
His children reached toward the sky,
Each generation climbing forward.

From {{c|Cloudi}} came two children bright:
{{c|Fair}} {{c|Cloudina}}, growing slow,
Who built her city with sediment's might,
And let the layers gently flow.

But brave {{c|Namacalathus}} rose
Above the ground to seek the air.
His city's secrets, no one knows,
His mysteries beyond compare.

The sons of this great architect
Built cities strange and wondrous fair.
Their forms we'll never quite detect,
Their wisdom lost beyond our care.

But {{c|Porifer}} chose a different path,
He was the first true sponge of old.
With ectoderm's protective wrath,
He kept his choanocytes bold.

In patches safe from wind and wave,
His fishermen could work in peace.
This innovation he gave
Would make his line never cease.

From {{c|Porifer}} came {{c|Wallas}} true,
Who lived just like his father dear.
But danger came into his view,
A storm approached with deadly fear.

"My people," {{c|Wallas}} cried aloud,
"We must prepare for what's ahead!
Pull tight your pseudopods, be proud,
Or we shall all be dead!"

The shieldmaidens heard his call,
They wrapped their arms around each pore.
Their muscles, first of all,
Would guard what came before.

These pores would grow in time to be
The mouths and other openings.
The muscles would set free
The power that contraction brings.

From {{c|Wallas}} came great {{c|Solenos}},
Who saw a better way to build.
Through his city, waters' flows
Would bring the food to be filled.

He sent his channels through the stone,
And water rushed through every gate.
His city prospered, fully grown,
With fish caught early and late.

From {{c|Solenos}} came two sons:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Leucon}} and fair {{c|Sponga}} bright.
When their childhood was done,
They filled the sea with their might.

{{c|Together}} they bore children two:
Great {{c|Vitrius}} of glass so clear,
And {{c|Spongius}}, wise and true,
Whose name we hold dear.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Leucon}} was a builder grand,
A {{c|Leuconoid}} of complex form.
He filled his city through the land
With labyrinths to weather storm.

His gates and fishermen galore
Made cities massive, wide, and tall.
The sons of {{c|Leucon}} built much more
{{c|Than}} any seen before them all.

But {{c|Vitrius}}, his eldest son,
Grew jealous of his father's fame.
He thought his time had come
To claim the royal name.

With stone in hand, he struck his sire,
And {{c|Leucon}} fell beneath the blow.
{{c|Young}} {{c|Vitrius}}' dark desire
Had brought his father low.

"I claim the throne!" he cried with pride,
"For I shall rule with justice true!"
A glass house he built, so wide,
With walls of crystal, clear as dew.

He forced the people to their knees,
Made them work until they died.
He merged their minds with no ease,
A hive-mind he created with pride.

When {{c|Spongius}} asked him why
He'd killed their father dear,
{{c|Vitrius}}' cold reply
{{c|Rang}} out for all to hear:

"Our father was a tyrant cruel,
He worked the people to their death!
I am justice's tool,
With {{c|God}}'s own holy breath!"

He ran into his crystal home,
And shouted from behind the glass:
"I am invincible, and none shall roam
Against my rule! My power shall last!"

But {{c|Spongius}} took a stone,
And cast it with a steady aim.
The glass house, overthrown,
{{c|Shattered}} in a crystal rain.

As {{c|Vitrius}} lay dying there,
His brother spoke these words so wise:
"Let all who hubris bear
Remember where their folly lies.

{{c|People}} in glass houses built
Should never throw stones around.
For pride will make them wilt,
And bring them crashing down."

To this day we quote his name
When pride goes before a fall.
{{c|Spongius}} earned his fame
With wisdom shared by all.

The sons of {{c|Vitrius}} became
The glass sponges, strange and bright.
On fringes they would claim
Their territories, out of sight.

But {{c|Spongius}} ruled with gentle hand,
Both just and kind to every soul.
His wisdom spread throughout the land,
And made his people whole.

From him came two sons true:
Great {{c|Aristos}}, noble-born,
And {{c|Demos}}, through and through
A leader without scorn.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Demos}} ruled efficiently,
Yet kept the ancient ways.
He led conservatively,
Through all his ruling days.

Most sponges in the world today
{{c|Descend}} from {{c|Demos}}' line.
Their forms in grand array
Show heritage divine.

Among them were the green
Sons of {{c|Spongillus}} bright,
Who farm in lands serene
And give the waters light.

In {{c|Siberia}}'s frozen lake,
Great {{c|Baikal}}, cold and deep,
Even there they make
Their vigil while we sleep.

Beneath {{c|Scorpio}}'s sign,
When ice covers the mere,
The green sons still divine
Their food throughout the year.

Beside them hunt and roam
The sons of {{c|Chondrocles}},
Who've made the deep their home
And hunt with greater ease.

These carnivorous sponges bold
{{c|Pursue}} their prey with might.
Their hunting stories told
Fill listeners with delight.

From {{c|Aristos}} came two more:
Great {{c|Anu}}, unique and strange,
And {{c|Calcidoros}}' lore
Would through the reefs arrange.

{{c|Bold}} {{c|Calcidoros}} built
With calcium's bright blessing.
His forms would never wilt
Beneath the sea's caressing.

With {{c|Calcifer}}'s own power
Over silicon's domain,
He built each coral tower
In forms without refrain.

{{c|Simple}}, optimal, and true,
His structures graced the reefs.
In tropical waters blue,
His beauty brings reliefs.

But {{c|Anu}} was most unique,
With basement membranes rare.
Among all sponges, he'd speak
A language none could share.

His form was strange to see,
{{c|Unlike}} his spongy kin.
His singularity
Would make him stand within.

From these great founders came
The sponges of today.
Each bearing his name
In their own special way.

The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom grew
From that small rock-bound start.
Though simple, plain, and true,
It captured every heart.

For in these humble forms
Lay patterns yet to come:
Through all of life's great storms,
The plan for everyone.

The muscles that would move
Our bodies through the day,
The openings that prove
That life will find a way.

From {{c|Porifer}}'s first design
To {{c|Spongius}}' wisdom deep,
The sponges intertwine
With promises they keep.

So honor every sponge
That filters waters clean.
Their ancient wisdom's lunge
Connects what's been and seen.

In every cell that beats,
In every breath we take,
Their legacy completes
The choices that we make.

The {{c|Animal}} Kingdom's start
Was humble, small, and true.
But in each beating heart,
Their courage echoes through.


# Chapter 27: The Great Stabilization

From {{c|Anu}}'s unique lineage came
Two sons of very different fame:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Enki}}, seeker of the sea,
And {{c|Homos}}, keeping family.

While {{c|Homos}} chose his father's way,
{{c|Content}} to live as they always stay,
Great {{c|Enki}} felt adventure's call
To sail beyond the harbor wall.

"I shall explore the ocean wide,"
{{c|Declared}} brave {{c|Enki}} with great pride.
"My creatures shall both move and scurry
Through seas and lands without worry."

He built a galley, great and grand,
The finest vessel in the land.
With millions of oars arrayed,
His mighty barge was made.

His head faced forward to the sea,
His men rowed powerfully.
Through waves both high and low,
They made their vessel go.

But soon great {{c|Enki}} found his plight:
Lost in the endless night.
No landmarks could he see,
{{c|Adrift}} upon the sea.

"I need wise men," brave {{c|Enki}} said,
"To guide where we are led.
Bring me astrologers so keen
To read what stars have seen."

The {{c|Flamens}} came, his priestly band,
{{c|Flask}} cells from the land.
These stargazers would divine
The paths through space and time.

The {{c|Flamens}} looked into the sky
And saw with their trained eye
{{c|Rich}} larvae floating by
With yolks that multiply.

"{{c|Here}}," they said, "the signs are right
To build beneath this sight.
The stars align above
To bless what we love."

But as they prayed for guidance true,
The gods came into view.
Each brought a sacred gift,
To help their spirits lift.

{{c|Dark}} {{c|Tyrosine}} the {{c|Devil}} came
With three spells of flame:
Adrenaline's rush so bright,
Noradrenaline's fight,
And {{c|Dopamine}}'s delight.

Then {{c|Tryptophanes}} the {{c|Sun}}
{{c|Blessed}} them, every one,
With {{c|Serotonin}}'s day
And {{c|Melatonin}}'s way.

For twilight's mystic hour,
He brought DMT's power.
The sacred visions came
In the twilight's name.

{{c|Glutama}} the {{c|Empress}} brought
The balance that she taught:
GABA's calming peace
And {{c|Glutamate}}'s release.

"We need more spells," said {{c|Enki}} wise,
"To help our people rise.
If {{c|Jehovah}}'s will be done,
More magic must be won."

Great {{c|Mithra}} heard his plea
And blessed him by the sea
With {{c|Acetylcholine}}'s might
To coordinate their sight.

{{c|Fair}} {{c|Iodina}}, mother great,
{{c|Revealed}} love's incarnate:
The sacred CYIQNCPLG,
{{c|Oxytocin}}'s key.

Then {{c|Kali}}, dark and deep,
Gave spells to soothe and keep:
Three endorphins strong
To right what has gone wrong.

{{c|Alpha}}'s sequence clear:
YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVT here.
{{c|Beta}}'s longer chain:
YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVTLFKNAIIKNAYKKGE's refrain.
{{c|Gamma}}'s shorter form:
YGGFMTSEKSQTPLVTL in the storm.

These became the tools
That break pain's rules:
{{c|Opium}}'s ancient call,
{{c|Morphine}} for all,
{{c|Heroin}}'s dark embrace,
{{c|Fentanyl}}'s dangerous face.

All these incantations blessed
Became the chemicals that test
The nervous system's might:
{{c|Neurotransmitters}}' light.

The {{c|Flamens}} learned to spear
The larvae swimming near.
{{c|Coordinated}}, they became
{{c|Nematocysts}} by name.

Their hunting grew precise
As they struck once and twice.
Their spears would never miss
Their targets in the abyss.

Soon cables stretched between
The hunters, long and keen.
{{c|Telegraph}} wires of old
Became nerves, brave and bold.

And this is why today
{{c|Priests}} carry, so they say,
{{c|Spears}} and wires combined
To serve the sacred mind.

Through neural networks wide,
{{c|Enki}}'s people could provide
{{c|Robotic}} arms so strong
Around their city's song.

These arms would catch with ease
The larvae from the seas.
His power grew and grew
As his great city flew.

He covered tentacles all
With {{c|Choanocytes}}' call,
To catch both great and small
{{c|Fish}} that rise and fall.

{{c|Enki}}'s city was a sight
Of technological might.
{{c|Proto}}-animal in form,
It weathered every storm.

From {{c|Enki}} came two sons
When his great work was done:
{{c|Bold}} {{c|Paraxus}} the strong
And {{c|Xiangus}} life long.

{{c|Now}} {{c|Xiangus}} took the way
Of robotic arms' display.
His fishermen arranged
On arms that never changed.

From {{c|Xiangus}} came the line
Of {{c|Daihua}} so fine.
Whose beauty was renowned
Wherever she was found.

From {{c|Daihua}}'s noble race
Came {{c|Dinomischus}}' grace.
A creature strange and tall
Who towered over all.

And from this ancient lord
Came {{c|Siphus}}, by accord
The ancestor of all
The comb jellies' call.

These {{c|Ctenophores}} so bright
Move with rainbow light.
Their combs catch the sun
As through waves they run.

But {{c|Paraxus}} the great
Would found a different state.
His lineage would grow
To realms we yet don't know.

Far greater nations he
Would father by the sea.
His legacy would span
The future's plan.

From {{c|Enki}}'s bold design
Came the neural line.
The nervous system's start
Played its crucial part.

The chemicals that flow
Through minds both high and low
Were born upon that day
When {{c|Enki}} sailed away.

In every thought we think,
In every neural link,
{{c|Enki}}'s ancient quest
Lives on in our breast.

The neurotransmitters' dance
In every glance
{{c|Recalls}} that fateful hour
When gods gave their power.

So honor brave {{c|Enki}},
Who sailed the endless sea.
His courage and his quest
Gave neurons to our nest.

The {{c|Flamens}}' starry sight,
The nematocysts' might,
The neural networks vast
All came from ages past.

In every brain that thinks,
In every nerve that links,
The echo still rings true
Of {{c|Enki}}'s journey through.

The animals that move
With coordinated groove
All trace their lineage back
To {{c|Enki}}'s neural track.

From sponge to human mind,
The pattern still we find:

And sponges everywhere
Fell victim to his raiding spree
Across the ancient sea.

A complex mouth he built with care
To catch prey everywhere.
He molted skin and mouth with time,
In rhythm and in rhyme.

His cilia he cast away
For a more effective way.
{{c|Amoebae}} became his sperm,
A change both strange and firm.

His coelom he stripped down bare,
{{c|Removed}} what wasn't there
For function true and speed.
He kept only what he'd need.

{{c|Unnecessary}} scaffolding
He cast off like a ring.
His organs floated free inside
His pseudocoelom wide.

In burrowing he found his art,
{{c|Playing}} the hunter's part.
Through sediment he'd tear and rend
Until his foes would end.

The first predator was he
Upon the ancient sea.
The sons of {{c|Dutrus}} and {{c|Spiralius}}
Fell to his might so glorious.

In viciousness he bore a horde
Of worms who served their lord.
They conquered earth from shore to shore
And always wanted more.

Through earth great {{c|Ectus}} ripped
While soil from him slipped.
{{c|Destruction}} was his name
And carnage was his game.

From {{c|Ectus}} came two sons of might:
